# Reply to Li et al.: Fluorinated liquid crystal monomers highlight a need for more data on emerging PFAS

**Authors:** Jennifer M Sun; Elsie M Sunderland

**Affiliations:** aHarvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138 | bSan Francisco Estuary Institute, Richmond, CA 94804

We thank Li et al. for highlighting fluorinated liquid crystal monomers (LCMs) as an emerging class of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in marine ecosystems that have thus far been overlooked (1). In our study of Subarctic marine mammal tissues, we found large declines in extractable organofluorine (EOF) driven by legacy PFAS phase-outs, but also a surprising absence of emerging PFAS. We hypothesized that many emerging PFAS classes exhibit differences in physiochemical properties, fate and transport, and exposure pathways compared to legacy PFAS. LCMs are an excellent example of one such class. In contrast with the ionizable, oleophobic structure of most legacy PFAS, LCMs are structurally more similar to some legacy persistent organic pollutants (POPs) (2), accumulate in marine mammal blubber, and likely undergo long-range atmospheric transport (3, 4). Some LCMs may also degrade to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), thereby contributing to rising global concentrations of this “ultrashort” PFAS (5).

Differences in the physicochemical properties of emerging organofluorine substances make it challenging to use a single analytical workflow to measure all substances. EOF and targeted PFAS extraction methods, and corresponding suspect screening analyses, are often not optimized for detecting neutral, semivolatile compounds like many LCMs. Further, recent work suggests that common EOF extraction and detection methods do not capture TFA (2, 6). TFA is highly polar and has been infrequently reported alongside standard targeted PFAS in past environmental measurements. The sheer number and diversity of organofluorine chemicals being discharged to the ocean, as highlighted by Li et al., underscores the need for a diverse toolbox of analytical methods when reconstructing the PFAS mass budget to identify compounds of greatest concern (1).

More broadly, the omission of LCMs defined as PFAS from recent measurements serves as a reminder that our understanding of environmental chemical contamination is defined by what we measure. Large unexplained fractions of EOF, such as those reported by Spaan et al. (7), motivate efforts to search for “emerging” PFAS classes and are often interpreted as “novel” PFAS. However, unexplained EOF can also be “legacy” classes of chemicals that have not yet been detected with targeted analyses. For example, another study of Northern Hemisphere marine mammals used a machine learning-based quantitation of suspect screening results to attribute a dominant fraction of unexplained EOF to legacy fluorotelomer carboxylic acids (FTCA) (8).

Virtually all prior environmental detections of LCMs have been reported in China, particularly around industrial sites and e-waste recycling centers (3). Although current LCM concentrations in South China Sea porpoises are lower than other legacy POPs and PFAS (4, 9), evidence of their persistence, bioaccumulation, potential toxicity, and ongoing use warrant further investigation. We agree with Li et al. that broader spatial assessments are urgently needed, especially given their potential degradation into TFA and the likelihood of atmospheric transport and deposition to the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. The diversity of such emerging PFAS classes and their degradation products further highlights the importance of a clear regulatory PFAS definition and class-based management approach that can encompass new classes as they continue to emerge (10, 11).
